burn_large_area.label: Burn larger than the person's hand

burn_white_charred.label: White, waxy, leathery or charred skin

burn_sensitive_area.label: Burn on face, hands, feet, joints or genitals

bleeding_not_stopping.label: Bleeding not stopping after 10 min of pressure

nose_injury.label: Nose bleed after a blow / broken nose

throat_face_swelling.label: Swollen lips, tongue, face or throat

cannot_bear_weight.label: Cannot move it or put weight on it

numbness.label: Numbness, tingling or pale/cold fingers or toes

rules.why: A baby is also a young child.
Unconscious for over a minute means the person is unresponsive.
No breathing = possible cardiac arrest.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Place the person on a firm flat surface. Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest: 30 compressions (about 5-6 cm deep, 100-120 per minute).
Give 2 rescue breaths if trained, then repeat 30:2. If untrained, do continuous compressions.
Use an AED (defibrillator) if one is available and follow its voice prompts. Do not stop until help arrives.

rules.why: An unresponsive person needs urgent professional care.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Check for breathing for up to 10 seconds. If NOT breathing, start CPR (30 compressions : 2 breaths).
If breathing, place in the recovery position (on the side, head tilted back) and monitor continuously.
Give nothing to eat or drink.

rules.why: Chest pain may be a heart attack.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Keep the person seated or half-sitting, calm and still; loosen tight clothing.
Follow the instructions of the emergency dispatcher. Be ready to start CPR if they collapse.

rules.why: Breathing difficulty can become life-threatening quickly.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Help the person sit upright and stay calm; loosen tight clothing and open a window for fresh air.
If they have a prescribed inhaler, help them use it.

rules.why: A seizure needs medical assessment.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Do not restrain the person and do not put anything in their mouth. Move hard objects away and cushion the head.
Note the time. When shaking stops, place on their side (recovery position) and stay with them.

rules.why: Heavy bleeding can cause shock.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Press firmly and directly on the wound with a clean cloth or your hand; do not release.
If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top - do not remove the first layer.
Lay the person down and raise the injured limb if possible; keep them warm.

rules.why: A minor burn can be treated with cooling and a clean dressing.
actions: Move away from the heat source. Remove rings, watches and tight clothing near the burn unless stuck to the skin.
Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes (minimum 10).
Cover loosely with clean cling film or a non-fluffy sterile dressing.
Do NOT use ice, butter, toothpaste or creams. Do NOT burst blisters.
Use simple over-the-counter pain relief according to the label if needed.

rules.why: Large blisters suggest a deeper (second-degree) burn.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Keep cooling the burn while waiting; do not burst the blisters.

rules.why: A burn larger than the person's hand is serious.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Keep cooling the burn while waiting and keep the person warm elsewhere on the body.

rules.why: White, waxy or charred skin indicates a full-thickness burn.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Do not remove clothing stuck to the burn.

rules.why: Burns on face, hands, feet, joints or genitals can cause lasting damage.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Cool with running water and keep the person calm; for face burns keep them sitting upright.

rules.why: Chemical and electrical burns can be deeper than they look.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Electrical: do not touch the person until the power is switched off.
Chemical: remove contaminated clothing and rinse with plenty of running water for at least 20 minutes.

rules.why: Burns in babies and children should always be checked.
actions: Have a doctor check any burn on a baby or young child, even if it looks small.

rules.why: A minor cut can be managed at home.
actions: Wash your hands (wear gloves if available).
Apply firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth or gauze for 10 minutes; raise the injured limb above heart level.
Once bleeding stops, rinse gently with clean running water and pat dry. Apply a sterile dressing.
Check that the tetanus vaccination is up to date (booster if >5-10 years for dirty wounds).

rules.why: Bleeding that will not stop after 10 minutes of pressure needs urgent care.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Keep applying firm pressure; add more cloth on top rather than removing it.

rules.why: Deep or gaping wounds may need stitches.
actions: Cover with a clean dressing and go to the clinic or hospital within a few hours for possible stitches.

rules.why: A stuck object may be plugging a major wound.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Do NOT pull the object out. Pad around it and bandage to hold it still.

rules.why: Bites carry a high infection and rabies/tetanus risk.
actions: Wash the bite thoroughly with soap and running water for several minutes and seek medical care the same day.

rules.why: Dirty wounds risk infection and tetanus.
actions: Clean thoroughly and see a doctor about tetanus protection.

rules.why: Pus, spreading redness or fever suggest infection.
actions: See a doctor - antibiotics may be needed.

rules.why: Blood-thinning medicines make bleeding harder to stop.
actions: Contact a doctor even for minor cuts and keep pressure for at least 15 minutes.

rules.why: A person who can cough is moving air - coughing is the best way to clear it.
actions: Encourage them to keep coughing. Do not slap their back while they cough effectively and do not put fingers in their mouth.
Stay with them. If coughing becomes weak or silent, or they cannot breathe, treat it as severe choking.

rules.why: A blocked airway is life-threatening.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Lean the person forward and give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If still blocked, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind, fist above the navel, pull sharply inward and upward.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the person becomes unconscious.
Even if the object comes out, the person should be checked by a doctor (thrusts can cause internal injury).

rules.why: A choking person who loses consciousness needs CPR.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Lower the person to the floor and start CPR (30 compressions : 2 breaths). Look in the mouth before each breath and remove any visible object.

rules.why: Infants need a different technique (replaces the adult steps of K2).
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
BABY under 1 year: sit down and lay the baby face-down along your forearm, head lower than the body, supporting the jaw.
Give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades. Turn the baby over and give 5 chest thrusts with two fingers on the centre of the chest.
Do NOT give abdominal thrusts to a baby. Repeat; start infant CPR if the baby becomes unresponsive.
Even if the object comes out, have the baby checked by a doctor.

rules.why: In pregnancy, thrusts are given on the chest (replaces the adult steps of K2).
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Lean the person forward and give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades.
If still blocked, give up to 5 CHEST thrusts (not abdominal): hands on the lower half of the breastbone, pull sharply inward.
Alternate until the object comes out or the person becomes unconscious (then start CPR). Get a doctor to check them afterwards.

rules.why: Most faints are brief and caused by a temporary drop in blood flow to the brain.
actions: Lay the person flat on their back and raise their legs about 30 cm. Loosen tight clothing and give fresh air.
Check breathing. Do not give food or drink until fully alert.
Let them stay lying for about 10 minutes, then sit up slowly before standing.
If it was the first time or had no clear cause (heat, standing up quickly, dehydration), see a doctor.

rules.why: Not waking within a minute is not a simple faint.
actions: If breathing, place in the recovery position; if not breathing, start CPR.

rules.why: Fainting with chest pain may be a heart problem.
actions: Do not let the person stand or walk.

rules.why: A head injury with a faint may mean concussion or bleeding in the skull.
actions: Keep the head and neck still; watch for vomiting, confusion or drowsiness.

rules.why: Fainting with convulsions needs urgent assessment.
Fainting during pregnancy should be checked.
actions: Lie on the left side and contact a doctor or midwife.

rules.why: A diabetic person may have low blood sugar.
actions: Once fully awake and able to swallow, give a sugary drink or glucose tablets. Seek medical advice.

rules.why: Repeated fainting needs a medical work-up.
actions: See a doctor soon to look for the cause.

rules.why: Fainting with breathing difficulty is a warning sign.
A quick recovery is reassuring.
actions: Keep the person hydrated and watch them for the next 24 hours.

rules.why: Most nosebleeds come from small vessels at the front of the nose.
actions: Sit upright and lean forward (do NOT tilt the head back).
Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10-15 minutes without letting go; breathe through the mouth.
Apply a cold pack to the bridge of the nose. Do not blow the nose for several hours.

rules.why: A nosebleed beyond 20 minutes needs medical control.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.

rules.why: A nosebleed after a blow may mean a broken nose or head injury.
actions: Get examined at a clinic or hospital.

rules.why: Blood thinners make bleeding harder to stop.
actions: Contact a doctor, especially if it does not stop in 10 minutes.

rules.why: Mild reactions (rash, itching, local swelling) are usually not dangerous.
actions: Move away from the trigger. For a sting: scrape out the stinger sideways (do not squeeze it).
Wash the area, apply a cold pack, and take an antihistamine according to the label.
Watch closely for the next hour - if breathing or swelling changes, treat as severe.

rules.why: Swelling of the face or throat suggests anaphylaxis.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Use an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector immediately if available - into the outer thigh; a second dose after 5 minutes if no improvement.
Lay the person flat with legs raised (sit them up if breathing is hard). Do not let them stand or walk.

rules.why: Allergy plus breathing trouble suggests anaphylaxis.
actions: Use an adrenaline auto-injector immediately if available - into the outer thigh.

rules.why: A fracture cannot be ruled out without an X-ray.
actions: Keep the injured limb still; support it in the position found with padding or a sling. Do not try to straighten it.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 20 minutes. Give nothing to eat or drink in case surgery is needed.
Go to the clinic or hospital for an X-ray.

rules.why: An open fracture risks severe bleeding and infection.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.
Cover the wound with a clean dressing; do not push the bone back or press on the bone ends.

rules.why: A deformed limb suggests a displaced fracture or dislocation.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.

rules.why: Numbness or a cold, pale limb suggests nerve or blood-vessel injury.
actions: Call emergency services now (Egypt ambulance 123, international 112) or ask someone nearby to call.

rules.why: Being unable to use the limb suggests a fracture.
actions: Do not walk on it - get an X-ray as soon as possible.
